articles.title: Johnny Depp Didn’t Just Leave Hollywood. He Left The US
articles.summary: Jack Sparrow isn't the only one who appreciates a private island.
articles.content:
Johnny Depp is officially back in Hollywood, at least as far as his career is concerned. His 2026 movie release , Ebenezer , just topped the domestic box office, marking his first major studio release in eight years. But while the actor is making his way back onto movie screens ( even for lesser pay ), he's apparently in no hurry to return to living in the United States. In fact, he's been spending most of his time somewhere that sounds an awful lot like a vacation destination.

I suppose having your own island makes avoiding the paparazzi considerably easier. And considering how much attention Depp's personal life has received over the years, I can understand why he'd want somewhere he can go about his day without somebody pointing a camera at him.

A wooden house, a yurt and somewhere to paint. Not exactly what I would have pictured for the man who spent years playing one of Disney's most recognizable characters, but I can appreciate the appeal.

His current living situation is especially interesting considering how frequently his family moved when he was growing up. Depp recalled relocating approximately 40 times during his childhood, particularly after his family moved from Kentucky to Florida. The constant changes made it difficult to settle in, and he described himself as an outsider.

Of course, his relationship with Hollywood became considerably more complicated in recent years. Depp stepped away from major American studio productions amid legal battles with his ex-wife, Amber Heard , including their highly publicized 2022 defamation trial. He continued working internationally, appearing in the French film Jeanne du Barry and directing Modi: Three Days on the Wing of Madness .

articles.title: 5 Times DC Changed a Superhero's Look and Got It Completely Wrong
articles.summary: Image Courtesy of DC Comics Superhero redesigns typically go one of two ways. Either the new costume is accepted and praised as a fresh take that captures the spirit of the character, or they are horrible looks that make you question if this is the same character at all. There are plenty of bad designs that simply aren't appealing, but […]
articles.content:
Wally West's Flash costume has always been a reflection of his journey. He started wearing a copy of Barry's, but designed his own updated version when he finally stepped out of his shadow. His 2016 Rebirth suit was beloved for combining his Kid Flash design with his Flash costume, but as sad as people were to see it go, it was hard to complain about Wally once again wearing his classic costume as he took over as the main Scarlet Speedster . However, the same can't be said for his costume for the first run in The Flash (2023), which involved big swathes of black, various specks of yellow, and a redesigned cowl.

Simply put, there's way too much going on with this design. Wally's costumes, and most iconic costumes in general, are typically simple but effective, as they are meant to be drawn in a variety of different ways, dozens of times a month. This is especially true for Wally, who is in constant motion and has a massive character investment in his costume specifically. The black bits also seem arbitrarily thrown on and break up the red in the strangest ways. The Flash has always been a character who rocked the brightest colors he could, and while this provides contrast, it doesn't really look right on Wally. Especially when he's at rest. Overall, a fine suit, but definitely not a Flash suit.

This redesign didn't just give us a new costume, but an entirely new character. Lobo's New 52 incarnation is infamous for revealing that the bastich we know and love was actually an imposter, insisting that the real Lobo was what looks to be an edgy teenager's original character. Lobo has one of the most distinctly '90s designs of all time, and that works in his favor. The original was a hulking, leather-jacket-wearing alien biker who rode a space motorcycle and used a massive spiked chain as a weapon. It's over-the-top and explosive to the point of circling back around to being cool. He works because he's a living relic who embodies all the zany, insane energy that saturated '90s comics.

The new Lobo threw all of that away, becoming a former palace guard who mourned the death of his planet and served as a bounty hunter while still maintaining that former sense of nobility, in a way. He has a much sleeker, more modern design that was meant to be cool and intimidating to a current audience. In other words, this version threw away everything that made Lobo actually work, keeping nothing fans actually went to a Lobo comic for. Worst of all, this design screams that it wants to be taken seriously, which is the last thing Lobo should ever be. It missed the entire point of why people like Lobo, and it's no mistake fans like to treat this like a painful memory from middle school.

Kyle is an artist at his core , and that means that he's never been shy about redesigning his costume. He was the first Green Lantern to massively change the uniform, adding a crab-like mask and armored forearms that felt fresh and unique at the time. His new design draws clear inspiration from that, effectively being a modernized version of it. It has all the same colors in all the same places, but the armor has been smoothed out and flattened into normal cloth. It's a much cleaner redesign and new take on his classic costume, and it's an awesome design for sure, but while it's a great look, it isn't a great look for Kyle.

Kyle has one of the most distinct styles in DC, and he's never been nervous to flaunt that, but this doesn't match that. Everything is too clean and derivative of what he's done before, to the point where it feels like someone trying to emmulate Kyle's instead of something he would make himself. The biggest show is in the mask. Kyle is famous for his unique brand of masks that would never fly with any other hero, but here he has a standard Green Lantern domino mask that's shrunk and even shows his eyes. The crab-mask is an essential part of Kyle's design, but this new one is clearly trying to be more standard, which goes against everything that makes Kyle's best designs work.

Doctor Fate's design has remained largely consistent throughout his history. Sure, there are definitely changes as his comics evolve, but beyond changing the Helm of Fate's shape from its earliest days, the vast majority of his designs only change details, not anything major about the suit itself. That is not the case for whatever the heck happened to him in the '90s. The Helm of Fate was melted down to forge a dagger and Ankh-shaped throwing stars. This came about when Kent and Inza Nelson, both of whom have been Doctor Fate before, hired Jared Stevens to retrieve the artifacts of Fate, only for them both to be rejected and killed, while Jared was imbued with magical energy and did the previously mentioned forging.

This is the single most '90s comic books thing I have ever seen. Words fail me when I try to describe this character, because it's like the people writing him had a checklist of every terrible trope from that era and made sure to get them all. Nothing about this screams Doctor Fate at all, and Jared even dropped the doctor title entirely. It was a clear attempt to draw in a new audience with dark, edgy action, but all it did was alienate every actual fan. This design was an attempt to entirely rewrite Doctor Fate's character, which is a slap in the face to everyone who actually enjoys the character, and definitely the worst type of redesign.

Tim Drake needs a new direction, that much is clear. He's been stuck in limbo for nearly two decades now, torn between his past as Robin and his need to find a new identity, unable to maintain the role while Damian exists. Brian Michael Bendis attempted to give Tim exactly the new identity he needed, but went about it in the worst way. Instead of Robin, Tim became Drake , donning a brown and yellow costume that couldn't look more generic if it tried. The biggest issue with this redesign is that it does nothing to actually give Tim what he needs while providing bland, boring alternatives.

For starters, the brown costume doesn't stand out at all. It's bland and boring to the point of being repulsive, and he even kept his Robin mask, which exacerbates the issue even more. The biggest problem, of course, is that Drake is just his name. Instead of giving him a new superheroic identity, they just chose his last name, which is the laziest way possible that doesn't actually carve him out anything new, as fans would just assume you were specifying who you mean when you say it. This wasn't even Tim's idea, as he stole it from an evil version of himself. This redesign didn't give Tim anything. If anything, it felt like it was made purposefully to call out all the problems he has while addressing none of them, leaving him in a worse spot than before.

Redesigns can be hard, but doing them right can be incredible, such as Batman's new blue costume in Batman (2025). Which recent DC redesign do you think works perfectly? Let us know in the comments below!

articles.title: Stranger Things’ Jamie Campbell Bower Reflects on Vecna, And His Comments Address A Fan Complaint [Exclusive]
articles.summary: Stranger Things star Jamie Campbell Bower, who played the fan-favorite villain Vecna/Henry Creel (and Mr. Whatsit and 001, along with a few other names) in season 4 and 5 of the show, has just shared some insights into the character that will likely make some fans very happy. Most recently, Bower has appeared in yet […]
articles.content:
However, working so closely with yet another foreboding villain— Charlie Vickers' Sauron —has given Bower cause to reflect a bit more on Vecna, about one year after Stranger Things concluded for good. Specifically, speaking exclusively with ComicBook , Bower reflected on the extent to which Henry/Vecna was a tragic character, which has been a hot topic in the fanbase since it was revealed that 001, Henry, and Vecna were one in the same in season 4. While there are still heated debates on both sides of this argument, Bower shared his perspective on Vecna as a villain, and his comments are likely to please many in the fanbase who have long taken issue with how Vecna's story ended in season 5. Check out Bower's exact comments below.

Speaking about whether he sees Vecna as tragic, Bower said, “There was a tragedy to him because there was, at the core of that character, a little boy, you know, who had an experience that changed his life dramatically. So, he wasn't created as the embodiment of evil. He was created as a person. That's who he was.” The latter, in particular, was in reference to Bower's Rings of Power co-star Vickers describing Sauron as “the embodiment of evil.” Even outside of the Rings of Power connection, however, this is a significant addition to the larger conversation about Henry Creel. Specifically, with the prequel play The First Shadow , audiences learned that young Henry had been controlled by the Mind Flayer just as Will Byers had once been.

This led to considerable sympathy for the character—even the evil adult version—because it was clear that Henry had been a victim as a child. Audience expectations were therefore high that Stranger Things season 5 would, at the very least, dive deeper into this more complex aspect of Henry/Vecna's history, if not redeem him, but in the end, many felt that they wanted more empathy for him than what was shown on screen. It's therefore nice to know that, at least from Bower's perspective (who seems like the expert on the matter), there was actually something tragic to Henry, and the fact that he had this experience as a child is an essential part of his story and of understanding the character.

Do you see Henry Creel/Vecna as a sympathetic character? Share your thoughts in the comments down below.

articles.title: At Least Robert Pattinson Looks the Part…According to Ian Fleming
articles.summary: The Bond author commissioned a sketch of 007 in the 1950s — and it bears an uncanny resemblance to a certain British actor currently being fitted for a tuxedo.
articles.content:
Well, it took nearly 70 years, and there were plenty of detours along the way, but Ian Fleming finally got the James Bond of his dreams — at least when it comes to jawline and nose shape.

None of the previous 007s — not Sean Connery, George Lazenby, Roger Moore, Timothy Dalton, Pierce Brosnan, or even Daniel Craig — looked anything like how the character's creator envisioned him. In Fleming's mind — at least according to the SMERSH dossier occasionally referred to in his books — Bond was about six-foot tall, 168 pounds, with black hair and blue eyes. For Pattison, that's check, check, check and check. But for the actors who proceeded him, not so much. blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-article-mid-article-uid0' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["mid-article1","mid-articleX","mid","mid-article"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-article") .addSize([[300,250],[2,2],[300,251],[620,350],[2,4],[4,2],[320,480],[620,366],[300,450],[4,4],[300,251]]) .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; }); Related Stories Movies James Bond Fans Already Complaining About Robert Pattinson: "Not Alpha Male" Movies How 'Twilight' Predicted Robert Pattinson's James Bond Casting

Connery and Lazenby had dark hair but brown eyes. Craig had blue eyes but fair hair (controversial coloring that inspired more than a few cheeky headlines when he was cast: "No Mr. Blonde, They Expect You To Dye"). Moore had blue eyes but his hair was shades too light. Brosnan came closest, with black hair and blue eyes. But it turns out Fleming had other criteria aside from basic coloring and measurements.

In fact, the author commissioned a portrait of Bond in the 1950s, years before the movies were launched, when a British newspaper purchased the rights to serialize the novels as a cartoon strip. To help the paper's illustrator nail down the look, Fleming hired an unknown artist to sketch 007's face according to his highly specific instructions ("I think we should avoid giving Bond an American-shaped head and a duck's haircut," he wrote in one note).

The result was a long angular face with heavy brows, a narrow nose, sharp cheekbones, thin lips and a firm, squared-off chin that looks uncannily like… Robert Pattinson . blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-dsk-tab-mid-article2-uid1' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["mid","mid-article2","mid-articleX"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-article2") .addSize([[300,250],[300,251],[620,350],[2,4],[4,2],[320,480],[620,366],[300,450],[4,4]]) .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; });

The funny thing is, the newspaper's illustrator, John McLusky, pretty much ignored Fleming's ideas and drew his own Bond with a much more rugged appearance — narrower eyes, a more expansive jawline, and a broad, cleft chin. In other words, a face that looked uncannily like… Sean Connery, who'd be cast in the part a half-decade later.

articles.title: An Unorthodox Star Wars Viewing Order Has Been Proposed By a Star Wars Icon & It Actually Makes Sense
articles.summary: Darth Maul voice actor Sam Witwer has just entered the chat regarding the proper Star Wars viewing order, and although his might be the most unique suggestion thus far, it actually makes sense—especially given the audience that he has in mind. Perhaps because George Lucas began with what is technically Episode 4 (although Lucas had […]
articles.content:
Almost as popular is the approach of watching the movies in chronological order, beginning with Star Wars: Episode I – The Phantom Menace and then going from there. Over the years, though, there have been many suggestions made, from how to incorporate the TV shows to watching Episodes 4, 5, 3, and then 6, and more. Amid the many perspectives on how one should best watch Star Wars is Witwer's new suggestion, which involves beginning with Star Wars: The Clone Wars . While that might sound like blasphemy, Witwer does actually have a good point. Check out his exact comments below.

Although Star Wars fans largely resisted The Clone Wars at first, likely in large part because it only arrived three years after Star Wars: Episode III – Revenge of the Sith , which was heavily criticized, it ultimately became seen as one of the franchise's best TV shows, if not the single best Star Wars TV show overall. From the introduction of Ahsoka Tano, who is now a fan-favorite character, to how much more significantly Anakin Skywalker is fleshed out as a character in the series, The Clone Wars has many merits that make in a solid addition to the galaxy far, far away. However, those aren't the reasons that Witwer believes The Clone Wars is the best place in the Star Wars timeline to start for young viewers.

Per Star Wars Holocron , Witwer said, “Here's my theory. I think you start with Clone Wars . And you don't have to start with all of it, just a lot of it. For kids, start with The Clone Wars . Get them used to what that world is and, more importantly, get them used to who Anakin Skywalker is. And then if you show them Episode IV and Obi-Wan's like, you know, Darth Vader killed your father, Anakin Skywalker, and then the kids are gunning for Darth Vader. And as long as you don't show them the prequels before that, they won't make that connection.”

Witwer continued, “So, then when you go to Episode V, you get ‘I am your father,' and then the kids are mind blown even more than you and me were mind blown, because they liked the guy, they mourned his loss, they went after the guy that killed him, to find out that's the same guy. And that's mind-blowing for them. And then once you hit Episode 5, then show them the prequels. And then at the end, which is really cool, when the droid [in Episode III] says [Padmé] is carrying twins, [the kid] is like pause, pause, pause, there is another?!” Witwer's comments are no doubt going to prove controversial, as this is certainly an unusual approach to Star Wars, and it means (in a way) usurping both the prequels and the original trilogy.

Even so, especially as an entry point for kids, The Clone Wars does make considerable sense, and Witwer actually makes great points for why, narratively, this would be an interesting approach.

What is your go-to Star Wars viewing order? Let us know in the comments down below.

articles.title: John Oliver Fills in for Tom Papa at Michael J. Fox Foundation Gala After FAA Ground Stop
articles.summary: Friday's four-hour halt to flights taking off across the U.S. also served as fodder for Josh Johnson's stand-up set, where he poked fun at last week's Microsoft outage as well.
articles.content:
By Saturday, air travel across the U.S. had resumed after the Federal Aviation Administration's four-hour nationwide ground stop on Friday .

But the effects of the stoppage were still unfolding, including in the entertainment world. At Saturday night's Michael J. Fox Foundation for Parkinson's Research gala in New York, host Denis Leary told the crowd that while they were fortunate that not many of the stars set to appear were affected by the ground stop, stand-up comedian Tom Papa, who was scheduled to perform at the benefit, was stuck in Los Angeles due to the grounding. blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-article-mid-article-uid0' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["mid-article1","mid-articleX","mid","mid-article"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-article") .addSize([[300,250],[2,2],[300,251],[620,350],[2,4],[4,2],[320,480],[620,366],[300,450],[4,4],[300,251]]) .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; }); Related Stories Music Grammys: Michael J. Fox, Tim Curry, 'Wicked: For Good,' 'The Pitt' Among Hollywood Nominees Lifestyle Baby2Baby Gala Fetes Demi Moore and Raises Over $20M for the Cause

In fact, he'd boarded his flight and was about to take off before the FAA ground stop on Friday.

But luckily the Michael J. Fox Foundation found another stand-up comedian in New York who could fill in: John Oliver . The Last Week Tonight host was a surprise performer at the star-studded annual benefit, where he initially joked that he was disappointing the audience after they'd already been told the scheduled comedian wasn't coming and Leary got the crowd thinking maybe Jon Stewart would be filling in since he mentioned that Oliver knows Stewart.

The FAA flight stoppage also served as fodder for fellow stand-up and Jon Stewart associate, Josh Johnson, as the Daily Show host used the beginning of his stand-up set to poke fun at Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy's reality TV past on The Real World: Boston and how the way he'd said a cyberattack wasn't responsible for Friday's ground stop (the FAA insisted the pause was due to air traffic control communication issues) made Johnson think it was definitely a cyberattack. blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-dsk-tab-mid-article2-uid1' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["mid","mid-article2","mid-articleX"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-article2") .addSize([[300,250],[300,251],[620,350],[2,4],[4,2],[320,480],[620,366],[300,450],[4,4]]) .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; });

Johnson also got some mileage out of the Microsoft outage that lasted from midday Thursday into early Friday , joking that it was great for people who were bad at their jobs, because they could simply claim they sent an email that no one could check.

“This is a dream come true for a low-tier employee,” he said.

Elsewhere at the event, which raised a record-breaking $6 million, former Late Show hosts Stephen Colbert and David Letterman made separate appearances where they jokingly stressed their ongoing relevance despite their CBS late night shows coming to an end.

Colbert joked, as he introduced a video of scientists working on medical treatments for Parkinson's as the Fox Foundation aims to find a cure for the neurodegenerative disorder, that being at the glitzy event at the Waldorf-Astoria in Manhattan made him “feel like [he has] a job.” And Letterman complimented the well-heeled audience in the hotel ballroom as he took a video on his phone to “prove to people that he's still in show business.”

The event ended with what's become a tradition at the gala of Fox joining the headlining musician onstage for a Back to the Future -inspired rendition of “Johnny B. Goode.” This year, Fox joined John Mayer and Brad Paisley along with No Doubt's Tom Dumont and Shoshana Bean. And Mayer, like Chris Martin , shared that the “new sound” Fox showed off as Marty McFly had made him want to pick up a guitar when he was a kid.

At the end of the benefit, Fox grabbed the microphone and joked that being able to perform with Mayer, Paisley and others was “definitely worth having Parkinson's for” and expressed a renewed commitment to finding a cure. blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-thr-article-mid-articleX-uid2' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["btf","mid-articleX","mid"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-articleX") .addSize([[300,250],[300,251],[620,350],[320,480],[620,366],[300,450],[4,4]]) .setLazyLoadMultiplier(2) .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; });

“We're gonna get it done,” he said.

Earlier on the red carpet , Fox's friends and former colleagues spoke about how happy they were that he'd been able to return to acting this year in Shrinking .

“When I saw the footage I said, ‘This is such a perfect pairing [of Fox and Harrison Ford's character who has Parkinson's], under a perfect premise,'” Leary told The Hollywood Reporter .

Fox's former Spin City co-star Alan Ruck suggested that the work done through Fox's foundation and improvements in Parkinson's treatments may have contributed to him being able to act again.

“I know that the medicine has improved a lot since the year 2000, because that's when he stepped away from Spin ,” Ruck offered. “Because it wasn't enough for him to go to work. It was debilitating. But the medicine has improved so much, now he's on Shrinking . He's done a number of things since then so that's encouraging that all of this research is paying off. And through this foundation, he is helping people's lives improve.”

And Leary, who'd worked with Fox on FX's Rescue Me , teased that he might have another acting gig for his friend.

“I think he's a great actor. So I jealously always want to create a character for him in whatever I'm doing. So I'm actually thinking about creating a character for him in this next thing I'm going to do,” Leary told THR .

Other stars who attended the event included Christopher Lloyd, Clark Gregg, Ted McGinley, Susie Essman, Ali Wentworth, George Stephanopoulos, Willie Geist and Terry Crews, whose wife Rebecca King Crews has been living with Parkinson's, going public with her diagnosis earlier this year .
